input: The current ophthalmologist's signed examination confirms non-physiological diplopia within 15 degrees of central fixation, reproduced during the assessment even though the driver says the two overlapping road-sign images sometimes merge after blinking; an older note reported comfortable reading at a desk, but that earlier description neither contradicts the current reproduced double vision nor establishes that a patch or new lenses have resolved it.

The current physician assessment explicitly describes the driver with established diabetes as acutely unwell with metabolically unstable diabetes, after vomiting and a measured glucose of 26 mmol/L prompted urgent assessment; the driver says the nausea eased after fluids, but the signed current review has not documented resolution of the instability, and a normal measurement copied from an earlier well visit is not evidence of the present metabolic state.

The treating specialist confirms vasovagal syncope during venepuncture, identifies the well-defined provoking factor and explicitly assesses recurrence while driving as unlikely; the driver describes nausea and sweating before that observed faint, but has not had unprovoked events, and the nurse records the specialist's current assessment separately from a draft referral that had initially listed arrhythmia as an unconfirmed differential diagnosis.

The audiologist's current signed report documents an unaided better-ear average of 35 dB over 0.5, 1, 2 and 3 kHz, with no aid worn during the measurements and audiometry explicitly completed; the driver sometimes turns the volume up for traffic updates in a noisy loading area, but the nurse separates that environmental complaint from the identified ear, frequencies and unaided testing conditions in the report.

The current physician assessment explicitly describes the driver with established diabetes as acutely unwell with metabolically unstable diabetes, after vomiting and a measured glucose of 27 mmol/L prompted urgent assessment; the driver says the nausea eased after fluids, but the signed current review has not documented resolution of the instability, and a normal measurement copied from an earlier well visit is not evidence of the present metabolic state.

The driver restarted antihypertensive tablets twelve days ago after a period of missed doses, and the current clinic letter still records persistent BP 188/108 mmHg on repeat checks; a four-week follow-up period has not yet been completed, the driver brings a booking confirmation rather than a specialist opinion, and occasional improvement on a home display cannot establish sustained control or the absence of relevant treatment problems.

A signed specialist review confirms a single blackout of undetermined nature after completed investigations, no recurrent blackout and an event-free interval of 5 years; appropriate specialist information is available for the commercial assessment, whereas the driver's recollection of feeling light-headed during a recent blood draw is explicitly documented as preserved awareness rather than another blackout, so it is not added to the confirmed event count.

The current doctor-reviewed series confirms persistent BP 179/103 mmHg while the driver is taking antihypertensive therapy, but the medication review also documents dizziness that impairs safe vehicle operation after the morning dose; although the driver feels better when sitting still in the interview, the nurse has no evidence that the side effect has resolved, and a proposed future dose change is not recorded as an accomplished treatment outcome.
